A graph that computes a picture

Fluxnode turns wired nodes into a live texture.

Drop source nodes — gradients, noise, checkers — wire them through mixers, warps, and filters, and watch an Output node render the result pixel-by-pixel as you tweak a slider. It's a real dataflow engine: typed ports, a topological evaluator, and cycle detection, all running in your browser.

What makes it feel alive

Fluxnode is a stateful pointer-driven application — a transform matrix, a graph model, an evaluator, and a renderer — the kind of tool you'd never assemble from page blocks.

Real dataflow graph

Nodes carry typed input and output ports. A connection is just an edge; the engine resolves the whole network into a single composed function every time you change anything.

Topological evaluation

Before rendering, Fluxnode sorts the graph with Kahn's algorithm so every node is computed only after its inputs are ready — no matter how you arrange the wires.

Cycle detection

Try to wire an output back into its own ancestor and the connection is refused. A reachability check runs before any edge is created, so the graph can never loop.

Pixel-accurate preview

The Output node exposes the final sampler — a pure (x,y,t) → rgb function. It's rasterized into an ImageData buffer, so what you see is exactly what exports.

Local-first & portable

Your flow autosaves to this browser as you work. Export the whole graph to JSON to back it up or share it, or export the rendered texture to PNG.

Infinite canvas + minimap

Pan and zoom toward your cursor on a scaling dotted grid. A live minimap shows the whole graph and your viewport; click it to leap across the network.

The node library

Fourteen node types in four families. Color signals are full samplers; number signals are scalars you can route into factor and level ports.

NodeGroupInOutWhat it does
GradientSource—colorTwo-stop linear gradient at any angle.
Solid ColorSource—colorA flat fill — handy for tinting and masking.
Noise FieldSource—colorFractal-brownian value noise with octaves & seed.
CheckerSource—colorTwo-colour checkerboard at any tile count.
Radial RingsSource—colorConcentric sine rings from the centre.
MixOperatorcolor color numcolorBlend A→B by a factor (slider or wired).
MultiplyOperatorcolor colorcolorMultiply / screen / add / difference blend.
Tint / HSVOperatorcolorcolorShift hue, scale saturation & brightness.
ThresholdOperatorcolor numcolorSoft cut on luminance into two colours.
WarpOperatorcolorcolorDisplace lookups by noise; optionally animate.
InvertOperatorcolorcolorMixable colour inversion.
PosterizeOperatorcolorcolorQuantize each channel into N bands.
Value / MathNumber—/numnumConstant & arithmetic (add, mul, sine…).
OutputOutputcolor—Gamma + vignette; renders the live preview.

How the engine works

Everything on the canvas is a plain, serializable record. A node stores its type, position, and parameter values; an edge stores the source node/port and target node/port it connects. Because the document is just data, the whole graph round-trips through localStorage and JSON without any special casing.

Each node type declares an evaluate(node, inputs) function. For color nodes it doesn't return a pixel — it returns a sampler: a pure function (x, y, t) → [r,g,b]. Operators simply close over their upstream samplers, so a five-node chain becomes five nested closures. When the Output node evaluates, it hands the editor a single composed function representing the entire pipeline. The preview then calls that function for every pixel and writes the bytes straight into an ImageData buffer.

To compute the whole graph in the right order, Fluxnode runs a topological sort (Kahn's algorithm): it counts incoming edges per node, repeatedly emits the nodes with none left, and decrements their neighbours. If any nodes remain when the queue empties, the graph contains a cycle — which the HUD reports. But you'll rarely see that, because connections are validated up front: before an edge is created, a reachability walk checks whether the target can already reach the source, and refuses the wire if so.

Why you'd never build this in a page builder

A page builder stacks static blocks. Fluxnode is the opposite: a single live surface where a graph data-structure, a scheduler, and a rasterizer cooperate on every pointer move. There are no sections to publish — there's one computation that updates the instant you drag a slider, drop a node, or pull a wire. That interactivity, with cycle-safe wiring and a real evaluator underneath, is exactly the kind of thing Gutenberg was never meant to express.
